# How it works

An explanatory piece for readers who know front-end frameworks and have read
Declare's homepage, the "Why" essay and the FAQ. Its premise: a Declare front
end is one complete artifact, and the runtime is what has to be true underneath
for that to hold. It follows one program from source to pixels: what the
compiler produces, what a click does, who decides where things are, where the
host begins, and how a Declare program meets code that isn't Declare.

The page is itself a Declare program, and its figures are live views rather
than pictures: morphs are sprung scalars, and the hit-testing figure reports
the runtime's own answers. Open it with `?render=canvas` and it is the same
page, drawn directly to pixels.

Sizes quoted here were measured 2026-09-18 from real `declarec` production
builds (gzip, default level).

include [ "../homepage/fonts.declare", "parts/figures.declare", "parts/kit.declare", "parts/hero.declare", "parts/compile.declare", "parts/ships.declare", "parts/click.declare" ]

// The page's palette, light and dark, as two token records. The App spreads
// one over a library preset below, so the few library widgets on the page find
// every token they read. The five layer hues (app, lib, run, ker, host) are the
// page's color code.

theme Paper [
    ground = #F4F6F7, panel = #FFFFFF, sunk = #EBEFF1, line = #D5DDE3,
    ink = #15202A, lead = #34434F, body = #2A3843, muted = #5B6B78, faint = #8796A2,
    codeBg = #E8EDF0,
    accent = #2F6BDE, accentHovered = #1F55BD,
    app = #2F6BDE, appSoft = #E3ECFC,
    lib = #0F9488, libSoft = #DDF3EF,
    run = #CF7B22, runSoft = #FBEBD8, runSoft0 = #FDF5EB,
    ker = #C23A5C, kerSoft = #F8E1E7,
    host = #6B7788, hostLine = #9AA6B3, hostSoft = #EDF0F3
    ]


theme Ink [
    ground = #0E1418, panel = #151D23, sunk = #1A242B, line = #26333D,
    ink = #E6ECF0, lead = #BBC7D0, body = #C9D3DA, muted = #8E9DA9, faint = #66757F,
    codeBg = #1E2931,
    accent = #6E9CF5, accentHovered = #93B6FA,
    app = #5F8FF0, appSoft = #17263F,
    lib = #2DB7A7, libSoft = #11302D,
    run = #E59A45, runSoft = #3A2A17, runSoft0 = #221C15,
    ker = #E3637F, kerSoft = #3A1C25,
    host = #8C98A8, hostLine = #5A6775, hostSoft = #1B242B
    ]


App [ appName = "How it works · Declare",

    // hosted: when a page mounts this program in an AppIsland (the homepage's
    // Architecture view), the host provides its appearance and type (read
    // here with hostProvided), and the page lengthens instead of this app scrolling
    // itself — so the host's own page scroll carries the article. Standalone,
    // the defaults hold and the app follows the system.

    hosted: boolean = { app.hostProvided("hosted", false) },
    headWeight: number = { app.hostProvided("headWeight", 600) },
    inDark: boolean = { app.hostProvided("dark", app.systemDark) },
    headTrack: number = { app.headWeight >= 900 ? -0.006 : app.headWeight >= 700 ? -0.014 : -0.02 },

    // this app's full height, exposed for the host to size its island to
    // (the host reads it as `island.exposed("docH", 0)`)

    exposes = ["docH"],
    docH: number = { this.page.y + this.page.height },

    scrolls = { app.hosted ? "none" : "y" },
    theme = { app.inDark ? ({ ...SanFranciscoDark, ...Ink }) : ({ ...SanFrancisco, ...Paper }) },

    // hosted, the app paints no ground: the host's own paper shows through

    fill = { app.hosted ? null : provided("theme").ground },

    // the site's face, as on the homepage

    uiFace: string[] = { Faces.helvetica },
    fontFamily = { app.uiFace },
    fontSize = 17,
    textColor = { provided("theme").body },

    // the two measures every edge on the page derives from

    col: number = { Math.min(680, app.width - 40) },
    wide: number = { Math.min(1060, app.width - 32) },

    // the first figure's two states: the reader switches between them

    heroMode: string = "looks",
    heroActual: boolean = { app.heroMode == "is" },

    // SELECTION IS PROVIDED ONCE, here, for the whole article. `selectable` is
    // a provided value, so a container opts its subtree in and each text leaf
    // reads the nearest provision — the type classes in the kit say nothing
    // about it, and a rich-text flow is selectable by its nature regardless.
    // The controls inside the figures are unaffected: every `Control` provides
    // `selectable = false` for its own label, which is the language's rule that
    // anything you activate is not copy.

    // The air above and below the article is the column's own padding. A padded
    // view has an inside: every child is placed from it, and the automatic
    // height counts the trailing inset back in, so `docH` measures the whole
    // article.

    page: View [ width = { app.col }, x = center, padding = [72, 0, 72, 0], selectable = true,
        layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 40 ],

        // ── the masthead ──────────────────────────────────────────────

        masthead: View [ width = 100%,
            layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 18 ],
            Eyebrow [ text = "Declare · runtime architecture" ],
            Title [ fontSize = { app.width < 700 ? 40 : 54 }, text = "How it works" ],
            Dek [ text = "A Declare front end is one self-contained artifact — small enough to hold in your head, strict enough for a machine to verify, rich enough for an ambitious application. This is what Declare’s runtime does to make that true." ]
            ],

        // ── the lede ─────────────────────────────────────────────────

        lede: View [ width = 100%,
            layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 22 ],
            Para [ html = "Declare asks you to believe something unusual about an application’s front end: that it is complete. Everything the interface does — where each box goes, how a paragraph wraps, what a click landed on, how a view becomes the next one — is written in the one program, as relationships rather than steps, so a machine can verify it and a person can read it. That puts a demand on what runs underneath: if the browser decided the layout, or the DOM routed the click, the program would not be complete. So the runtime makes those decisions itself, once, and hands the browser what it does best." ]
            ],

        // ── the first figure ─────────────────────────────────────────────

        fig1: Figure [
            top: View [
                Segmented [ x = center, width = 300, height = 32,
                    value = { app.heroActual ? "is" : "looks" },
                    items = { [ ({ id: "looks", label: "What it looks like" }), ({ id: "is", label: "What it is" }) ] },
                    commit(v: object) { app.heroMode = "" + v }
                    ]
                ],
            Plate [ pad = 0,
                stage: HeroStage [ k = 0,
                    Spring [ attribute = k, to = { app.heroActual ? 1 : 0 }, stiffness = 60, damping = 14 ]
                    ]
                ],
            keys: View [
                legend: View [ x = center,
                    layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = x, spacing = 16 ],
                    Key [ hue = { provided("theme").app }, label = "App" ],
                    Key [ hue = { provided("theme").lib }, label = "Library" ],
                    Key [ hue = { provided("theme").run }, label = "Runtime" ],
                    Key [ hue = { provided("theme").ker }, label = "Kernel" ],
                    Key [ hue = { provided("theme").hostLine }, label = "Host" ]
                    ]
                ]
            ],

        // ── 01 · The compiler ────────────────────────────────────────

        compile: Section [ num = "01", head = "Why a program can be checked",
            Para [ html = "The compiler is where completeness is enforced. It parses the brackets into a tree, resolves every name to an explicit path, extracts what every <code>{ }</code> body reads, and type-checks each body as TypeScript against the real interface of every class — so an attribute that doesn’t exist, or a relationship that reads something it can’t, is an error before anything runs. What it emits is not code that builds a UI but a description of one: the tree, a graph of which value reads which, and, for every body that is plain arithmetic, bytecode for a small stack machine. One line of the homepage’s bouncing-ball demo, compiled:" ],
            Trace [ ],
            Para [ html = "Because the program is data, it can be questioned as data. The Inspector on any page here — ⌥⌘D — reads this same graph: click a value and it shows the body that produced it, everything that body read, and their live values. The same completeness is what lets an AI’s work be checked: the compiler, the Inspector and verify all read one description of the whole interface, not a guess pieced together from files." ]
            ],

        // ── 02 · What a click does ───────────────────────────────────

        run: Section [ num = "02", head = "Why nothing re-renders",
            Para [ html = "When a handler writes an attribute, nothing updates yet. When the handler returns, the runtime performs one update — a <b>settle</b>: everything that read what changed is recomputed, and whatever that changes in turn, until nothing more does; only then is the host told what moved. If you know React, it is the nearest thing to a commit, except that nothing was rendered to compare against. The meter below is live: raise its level, then step through what your click set in motion." ],
            Figure [
                ClickFig [ ]
                ],
            Para [ html = { "Which view is under the pointer, and whether this was a click or the start of a drag, are the runtime’s answers, not the browser’s — one implementation under a finger or a pointer, on every renderer. And the settle itself runs in a kernel: one C file of about " + FIGURES.kernelLines + " lines that holds the graph’s tables and evaluates the compiled arithmetic, shipped as WebAssembly (" + Math.round(FIGURES.kernelWasmGzipKB) + " KB gzipped) and linked natively on the Mac. A frame that only moves geometry never enters JavaScript." } ]
            ],

        // ── 03 · Motion and layout ───────────────────────────────────

        motion: Section [ num = "03", head = "Why every animation can be interrupted",
            Para [ html = "A <code>Spring</code> is an attribute with a target; each frame it writes its next value, and that write is a settle like any other. Nothing about animation is special-cased, so a new target mid-flight is simply the next write: the spring retargets from wherever it is, and everything that read it follows. Interruptibility isn’t a feature of an animation system; it is what a reactive graph does when you write to it." ],
            Para [ html = "Every box is decided before the host hears of it — by arithmetic over attributes, by a layout (a class with one method, <code>place()</code>), or by the content’s own size. Text is the one place the host contributes a number, the width of a glyph; wrapping and height are the runtime’s, so a paragraph breaks into the same lines on every renderer. Because the runtime placed every box, it also answers the inverse question — what is under this point — and that one answer decides hover, press, and where a drag lands." ]
            ],        // ── 04 · Why it’s fast ───────────────────────────────────────

        fast: Section [ num = "04", head = "Why it’s fast",
            Para [ html = "Because the compiler hands over the whole graph up front, the runtime doesn’t have to discover anything as it runs. Its reactive core (the graph, the settle, and the arithmetic of layout, springs and visibility) is a small C kernel: WebAssembly in the browser, linked natively on the Mac. Bodies that are plain arithmetic arrive as bytecode the kernel evaluates itself, without returning to JavaScript." ],
            Para [ html = "Moving the core there cut update time by 42–53% on every platform measured (Chrome, iOS Safari and the Mac host), and a window drag’s by 81–93%. The rules evaluated didn’t change; each one simply costs less." ]
            ],

        // ── 05 · One program, three hosts ────────────────────────────

        hosts: Section [ num = "05", head = "One program, three hosts",
            Para [ html = { "Everything above happens on one side of a single interface, <code>Surface</code> — " + FIGURES.surfaceMethods + " methods such as <code>setX</code>, <code>setFill</code> and <code>setText</code> that the runtime calls and a backend implements. The DOM backend keeps an element per view and hands the browser what it does best: real text, the page’s own scroll, links, native fields. The canvas backend draws the tree directly to pixels. The Mac host is a Swift application with no web engine in it, applying each settle to Core Animation layers. Drawing (<code>draw(d)</code>) records rather than paints, so each host replays the same recording its own way." } ],
            Para [ html = "Below, the calendar’s build drawn to scale by gzipped bytes: switch hosts and one block is exchanged while everything else holds still. Beneath it, the same desktop program on each host." ],
            f4: Figure [
                sf: ShipsFig [ ]
                ]
            ],

        // ── 06 · Living alongside other code ─────────────────────────

        islands: Section [ num = "06", head = "Living alongside other code",
            Para [ html = "A web page embeds a Declare app with one attribute on a sized element; inside a Declare program, a <code>DOMIsland</code> gives a video player, an editor or a React widget a box of its own, and an <code>AppIsland</code> hosts another Declare program — this article is one, inside the homepage. In every direction the contract is the same: values provided, values exposed, and messages posted both ways." ]
            ],

        // ── 07 · Still a web page ────────────────────────────────────

        why: Section [ num = "07", head = "Still a web page",
            Para [ html = "In a browser a Declare app is a web page, not an imitation of one: text selects and finds, fields are native, scroll is the page’s own, links ⌘-click and Back tells the truth, and a crawler reads a static extraction from a plain host. What keeps the runtime honest is the second rendering: the DOM and the pixel renderer are held to the same picture on every change." ],
            links: View [ width = 100%,
                layout: WrappingLayout [ spacing = 22, rowSpacing = 10 ],
                Text [ fontSize = 15, fontWeight = medium, link = "apps/architecture/architecture.declare?render=canvas",
                    textColor = { this.hovered ? provided("theme").accentHovered : provided("theme").accent },
                    text = "Reopen this page on the canvas renderer →" ],
                Text [ fontSize = 15, fontWeight = medium, link = "apps/architecture/architecture.declare?viewer=reader",
                    textColor = { this.hovered ? provided("theme").accentHovered : provided("theme").accent },
                    text = "Read this page’s source →" ]
                ]
            ],

        colophon: View [ width = 100%,
            layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 10 ],

            // nothing here claims a width — a y-axis stack never does — so the
            // rule derives its own from the parent's content box

            Divider [ ],
            Small [ width = 100%,
                text = "This page is a Declare program; every figure on it is made of views. Sizes are measured from declarec production builds, gzipped at the default level, each time the site is built." ]
            ]
        ]
    ]
